title.narrative: Mozambique Primary Health Care Strengthening Program

description.narrative: The Program Development Objective is to improve the utilization and quality of reproductive, maternal, child and adolescent health and nutrition services, particularly in underserved areas.

The objective of Primary Health Care Strengthening Program Project for Mozambique is to improve the utilization and quality of reproductive, maternal, child, and adolescent health and nutrition services, particularly in underserved areas. Program will focus on three thematic areasof the Investment Case (IC): (i) enhancing coverage, access, and quality of primary health care services, including high-impact supply and demand-side interventions, with a focus on underserved areas; (ii) strengthening the health system for improved stewardship, financial sustainability, expenditure efficiency and equity, and gender responsiveness of service delivery, together with improved Civil Registration and Vital Statistics systems; and (iii) enabling Ministry of Health to effectively manage the implementation of the IC, through technical assistance, capacity development, monitoring and evaluation (M&E), and Health Partners coordination activities. The program will specifically support improvements in Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAH) outcomes, in addition to systemic improvements to equitable distribution of health resources and accountability to results at all levels.

title.narrative: Number of health facilities providing Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care

comment.narrative:
<p>Originally, this IRI included measurement of the number of facilities providing basic (BEmONC) services also - with the baseline from the 2014 SDI being BEmONC 68 and CEmONC 33.</p>

<p>During Program implementation, MISAU reported data from Provincial acreditation processes that was not verifiable. UNFPA was supporting accreditation processes but this work had been delayed and data was not available. Hence, the 2021 Restructuring formally revised the IRI to only report number of facilities prviding CEmONC services, as this was reported through routine MISAU data.</p>

<p><em>Originally, there were two additional IRIs for "service readiness and availability"- measuring percentage of district hospitals with uninterrupted water supply and electricity; and availability of essential reproductive and maternal health medicines in district and rural hospitals.  Both o these IRIs were deleted at the 2021 Restructuring as they were supposed to be measured through SDI surveys.</em></p>

<p> </p>

Percentage of children aged 0-24 months receiving a Nutrition Intervention Package in eight priority provinces (with the prevalence of stunting of above 35 percent)

comment.narrative:
<p>The original <u><em>six Provinces</em></u> were <u><em>Cabo Delgado, Manica, Nampula, Niassa, Tete, and Zambezia</em></u></p>

<p>At the 2019 AF and Restructuring, the scope of the indicator was expanded to include <u><em>two additional districts</em></u> (<u><em>Inhambane and Sofala</em></u>); and indicator statement was modified for greater clarity and focus on <u><em>stunting above 35 percent</em></u>.</p>

<p>In 2020, delays in the supply of critical inputs and the cessation of some activities during theandemic resulted in coverage of 4% with the modified NIP (under the target of 15 percent).? </p>

<p>For 2021, MISAU reported?achieving a coverage of 16 percent (under the target of 40 percent).  MISAU contracted an?NGO?to support implementation activities for 2022. </p>

<p>For 2022, MISAU reported a coverage of 23 percent, i.e. slightly more than 50 percent of the target? (target was 40 percent). This result was validated by the IVA.? </p>

<p>For 2023, MISAU reported a coverage of 55%. </p>

<p> </p>

Percentage of secondary and technical schools offering sexual and reproductive health services (information and contraceptive methods)

comment.narrative:
<p>The original IRI statement referred to "percentage of schools".  The 2019 Restructuring clarified the target group as "percentage of secondary and technical schools".</p>

<p>In 2019, MISAU reported 233 (32 percent) of 710 secondary and technical schools received sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services. However, only 55.76 percent?of a sample of 52 schools (22 percent) documented meeting all the criteria (including the provision of contraceptive methods, counseling, community engagement through school councils, and monitoring). </p>

<p>In 2020, MISAU reported meeting the target of 19 percent of technical and secondary schools offering SRH services. However, only 67.87 percent of the sample of 28 schools were found to meet the revised criteria.? </p>

<p>In 2021, MISAU reported that 38 percent of secondary and technical offered SRH services. </p>

<p>For 2022, MISAU reported that 61% (433) of secondary and technical schools offered SRH services, against the restructured target of 50 percent. The IVA validated an achievement of 51.76 percent.</p>

<p><em>In 2023, MISAU reported that 58 percent ofecondary and technical schools offered SRH services. </em></p>

Number of lagging districts (as defined in the IC) that provide four doses of intermittent preventive treatment of malaria to at least 60 percent of pregnant women
Number of lagging districts (as defined in the IC) that provide four doses of intermittent preventive treatment of malaria to at least 60 percent of pregnant women

comment.narrative:
<p>The indicator for measuring improvement of quality of RMNCAH services underwent several changes during implementation, all of which were formalized through Restructurings.</p>

<p>The 2021 Restructuring replaced the two original indicators (PDOs 4 and 5) with a single one (PDO 4), as a proxy indicator for quality of RMNCAH services.  In 2021, the indicator was "reaching at least <u><em>70 percent </em></u>of pregnant women", and this was revised (at the 2023 Restructuring)  to "reachig at least <em><u>60 percent </u></em>of pregnant women"; with the baseline remaining unchanged of 10 lagging districts.</p>

<p>Following the revision to a single quality indicator (PDO 4), progress was as follows:</p>

<p>In 2021, MISAU reported 11 districts?meeting the target. </p>

<p>In 2022, MISAU reported 11 districts, however the IVA (following a quality control exercise) reported that  21 districts reached the target. </p>

<p>In 2023, MISAU reported an achievement of 25 districts.</p>

title.narrative: Number of districts, out of the 42 identified as lagging in the Investment Case, with at least 85 percent institutional deliveries

comment.narrative:
<p>The original PDO was: Percentage of institutional deliveries in 42 lagging districts as defined in the IC. The baseline was 66.1 percent (SISMA 2016) and end target was 82.20 percent (30 Dec 2022).</p>

<p>The percentage of institutional deliveries is defned as the total number of pregnant women who delivered their babies in a health facility in a priority district out of the total number of expected childbirths in the same district in a year.</p>

<p>At the 2019 AF and Restructuring the baseline was increased to 71 percent (SISMA 2017) and end-target to 85 percent. 86 percent was achieved at end-2018.  </p>

<p>The 2021 Restruturing revised PDO 1 and DLI 1 statements, with a baseline of 28 districts, and setting an end-target of 37 districts (31 December 2022) recording at least 85 percent of institutional deliveries.</p>

<p>In 2020 and 2021, 32  and 31 lagging districts respectively reported at least 85 percent of institutional deliveries. </p>

<p>For 2022, 33 districts reported meeting the end-target of 37 districts; and this was confirmed by the IVA.  </p>
